A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training

 

Kartikeya Bhardwaj 1  Mohammed Almousa 1  Chaitanya Mullapudi 1  Ananth Balasubramanian 1  Nithin Ramesan 1  Tuc Nguyen 1  Harris Teague 1 

††footnotetext: 1Qualcomm AI Research. Qualcomm AI Research is an initiative of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. Correspondence to: Kartikeya Bhardwaj <kbhardwa@qti.qualcomm.com>.
Preprint. Copyright 2026 by the author(s).
Abstract

Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3%\bm{6.3\%} average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7%\bm{7.7\%} better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

1 Introduction

Quantization has become the de facto strategy for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language models (VLMs) on resource-constrained systems such as phones and laptops Nagel et al. (2021); Gong et al. (2025). To address the substantial memory footprint, power consumption, and cycle cost of inference of generative models, quantization reduces the precision of weights and activations from a higher bitwidth to a significantly lower bitwidth. This reduction in precision introduces quantization errors which result in noisy model outputs and an associated accuracy degradation in the real-world applications Song et al. (2026). The prevailing paradigm that current hardware supports is quantization bitwidths in the range of 2 to 4 bits. The lower the bits, the worse the quantization error, albeit with a significantly better energy-efficiency. Although many advanced techniques exist that address 4-bit precision Lin et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025a); Sun et al. (2020); Frantar et al. (2022); Ashkboos et al. (2024), even lower bitwidth, such as 2-bit quantization, remains a critical challenge Liu et al. (2025b); Li et al. (2026); Lee et al. (2025). Hence, investigating newer quantization techniques to address 2-bit precision for weights is of paramount importance.

For such low precisions, training-free methods known as Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) have not been effective at recovering the quantization error Liu et al. (2025b); Yi et al. (2026). Consequently, Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) techniques have emerged as the standard methods to convert a pretrained floating point model to a 2-bit weight model Song et al. (2026). Various QAT methods target different challenges: LSQ Esser et al. (2019) proposes a learned scale as well as improvements to the gradient computation to improve the QAT convergence. ParetoQ Liu et al. (2025b) proposes a new symmetric integer grid for 1.58- and 2-bit models. WinQ Li et al. (2026) addresses the presence of saddle points or flat regions in the quantized loss surface. Progressive quantization methods such as UPQ Lee et al. (2025) focus on converting a model from a floating point precision to 2-bits in multiple stages, e.g., going from floating point model to 4-bits first, and then eventually quantizing the model to 2-bits.

Most QAT techniques in the literature result in an abrupt change in bitwidth, either from floating point directly to 2-bits Liu et al. (2024a); Chen et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025b); Li et al. (2026); Yi et al. (2026), or as in the case of UPQ Lee et al. (2025), from floating point to 4-bits first and then suddenly to 2-bits. Once the desired bitwidth is reached, the model is trained with no further changes in precision. It is known that low-bit quantization loss surfaces usually consist of highly flat surfaces Li et al. (2026) due to the nature of quantization itself. Hence, when we optimize on a fixed bitwidth, the optimization may get stuck in those flat portions of the loss surface. Indeed, increasing the bit-precision of the weights can make the loss surface less flat and can make it easier for the optimization to escape saddle points. To this end, we hypothesize whether a dynamic bitwidth during the QAT can be a solution to this problem. Importantly, since abrupt changes in bitwidth can destabilize the training, we need a solution that makes gradual changes to the bitwidth as the training progresses.

Therefore, we ask the following key questions in this paper: During QAT, can we dynamically relax the bitwidth of a model in a continuous fashion? That is, instead of discrete (abrupt) integer changes in the number of bits, can we change the bitwidth in a continuous (floating point) domain? If yes, how do we implement a floating point bitwidth and what does it even mean?

To answer the above questions, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT problem. The key idea behind RelaxQAT is to create a schedule for the bitwidth and change the underlying QAT equations, so that the extreme values in the model weight distributions become floating points which slowly turn into integers during the training. Importantly, the dynamically changing bitwidth also dynamically changes the number of quantization bins, which helps the model escape saddle points and reach a better training loss. With extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our method achieves significantly better benchmark accuracies on a variety of vision-language and natural language tasks. Of note, our work focuses only on channelwise quantization since it remains one of the most hardware-efficient quantization schemes, and is highly relevant to deploying large generative models on constrained hardware such as Neural Processing Units (NPUs).

Overall, we make the following key contributions:

  1. 1.

    We propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT. To our knowledge, we are the first to dynamically vary the bitwidth in a floating point domain and the resulting number of quantization bins during the QAT.

  2. 2.

    We provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance.

  3. 3.

    For the challenging case of 2-bit weight only quantization, we demonstrate that RelaxQAT achieves the state-of-the-art accuracies on a variety of vision-language and natural language benchmarks. We show an improvement in average accuracy of up to 6.3%\bm{6.3\%} on vision benchmarks compared to the leading QAT baselines. On natural language tasks, we show up to 7.7%\bm{7.7\%} better average accuracy. In total, we conduct experiments on five models of various sizes (0.6B to 4B), spanning two VLMs, three LLMs, and multiple model (Gemma and Qwen) families. We consider five leading QAT baselines and each model is trained on 10B tokens.

  4. 4.

    Finally, we also show a proof-of-concept that RelaxQAT can be used for other bitwidths such as ternary (1.58-bit) quantization. We show up to 4.2%\bm{4.2\%} accuracy gains for this quantization scheme.

2 Related Work

We review briefly important quantization methods from the literature to set the stage for our proposed RelaxQAT algorithm. One of the early work in low-bit quantization was the Learned Step Quantization, introduced by Esser et al. (2019). LSQ’s key innovation was to treat the quantization step size itself as a learnable parameter .Choi et al. (2018), proposed learning activation clipping thresholds during training while Bhalgat et al. (2020) proposed learning both scale and offset.

Building on LSQ, Liu et al. (2025b) proposed ParetoQ which introduced Stretched Elastic Quantizer (SEQ) for ternary and 2-bit quantization. It is shown that although LSQ performed well in higher-precision (e.g., 4-bit quantization), its effectiveness degrades significantly in the extreme low-bit regimes. To address this, SEQ employs a more symmetric quantization grid, leading to improved performance. Inference scaling laws for models w.r.t quantization have been extensively studied in Dettmers and Zettlemoyer (2023), Šubić and Cozzini (2026), and Liu et al. (2025b).

BitNet was proposed in Hugging Face (2024), which introduced the idea of gradually transitioning model weights towards the target low-bit representation through a predefined schedule (e.g., linear schedule). This is accomplished by linearly combining the latent weights with appropriately scaled version (based on a schedule) of difference of FP latent weight and the desired quantized weight. However, in our proposed RelaxQAT, the bitwidth itself changes based on a schedule. Other follow up works in Bitnet w.r.t activation quantization, 1-bit optimzation and efficient inference are detailed in Wang et al. (2024), Wang et al. (2025c), Wang et al. (2025d).

Li et al. (2026) investigates the root cause of slow convergence observed in quantization-aware training (QAT) for extreme low bit quantization. It is shown that low-bit training tends to become trapped in flat regions around saddle points of the loss landscape, resulting in slower optimization. To mitigate this issue, an optimization strategy is proposed that periodically interpolates the quantized weights with the latent weights to escape the saddle point. Further, Xu et al. (2025), Xu et al. (2026),Wei et al. (2022), Lv et al. (2026), Shao et al. (2024), Lee et al. (2024), Wang et al. (2025b), Wang et al. (2025a) analyse several low-bit training methods and how outlier-aware quantization schedules improve convergence and accuracy at extreme bit widths.

A direction closely related to our proposal is the progressive quantization framework introduced in Unifying Block-wise PTQ and Distillation-based QAT for Progressive Quantization (UPQ) Lee et al. (2025). UPQ proposes a two-stage quantization pipeline in which a full-precision model is converted to an intermediate representation (e.g., INT4) using block-wise post-training quantization (PTQ), followed by INT2 QAT initialized from the intermediate checkpoint. In contrast, the proposed RelaxQAT generalizes the notion of progressive quantization by replacing the fixed transition (FP to INT4 to INT2) with a continuously evolving bit schedule. We hypothesize that this continuous transition enables a smoother optimization trajectory as shown next.

3 Proposed RelaxQAT

RelaxQAT consists of two parts: (i) set bitwidth using a smooth schedule during training, and (ii) modify existing quantization equations such as Stretched Elastic Quantizer (SEQ) Liu et al. (2025b) to make sure the extreme values of the weight distribution become floating points so they can smoothly vary as the bitwidth changes. We describe these components below.

3.1 Bitwidth Schedule

The bitwidth (btb_{t}) at training step tt is given by:

bt=bs−(bs−be)​sin​(π2​ω),ω∈[0,1]b_{t}=b_{s}-(b_{s}-b_{e})\text{sin}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\omega\right),\ \ \ \ \omega\in[0,1] (1)

Here, bsb_{s} and beb_{e} are the starting and ending bitwidths, respectively, and ω∈[0,1]\omega\in[0,1] dynamically changes during training. Eq. (1) states that when ω=0\omega=0, we get the starting bitwidth (bsb_{s}), and when ω=1\omega=1, we get the desired final bitwidth (beb_{e}). Typically, the ω\omega starts at 0 and ends at 1 and then follows a cyclical pattern. Before the end of the training, we keep ω=1\omega=1 to ensure that the model finetunes in the desired beb_{e} bitwidth for a prolonged time.

An example of our proposed bitwidth schedule is shown in Fig. 1(a). We typically start with a half cycle going from bitwidth bsb_{s} to beb_{e} over maximum schedule steps (msm_{s} training steps). For instance, in Fig. 1(a), bs=4b_{s}=4, be=2b_{e}=2, ms=1200m_{s}=1200). This corresponds to ω\omega changing from 0 to 1. After this half cycle, we can have nn full cycles (n∈{1,2,3,…,…,N}n\in\{1,2,3,...,\ldots,N\}) where the ω\omega cycles from 1 to 0 and then back to 1. This results in bitwidth changing from beb_{e} to bsb_{s} and then back to beb_{e}. As shown in Fig. 1(a), at step 3000, the quantization bitwidth starts to relax from 2 bits to 4 bits (by step 4200, since ms=1200m_{s}=1200 and n=1n=1) and then goes back to 2 bits by step 5400. The intuition behind adding one or more full cycles after the initial half cycle is to help the optimization escape any flat regions that it might be stuck in. We empirically validate that the additional full cycles indeed help improve the RelaxQAT performance.

It is important to note that Eq. (1) leads to a slowly changing bit precision which can be a floating point value. Moreover, the gradient of the proposed schedule is 0 whenever it approaches 2-bits. This helps us to ease into 2-bit precision instead of a sudden change in bitwidth. In contrast, existing methods either (i) perform progressive quantization to train the model in stages and abruptly change the bitwidth (e.g., UPQ Lee et al. (2025), see Fig. 1(b) blue line around step 2000), or (ii) keep it the same throughout the QAT after directly reducing it from the floating point precision (e.g., ParetoQ Liu et al. (2025b), see Fig 1(c) red line).

Our hypothesis is that the relaxation in bitwidth can help the optimization escape the flat regions in the quantization loss surface. Further, a sudden change in bitwidth in methods such as UPQ can cause the loss to increase suddenly, and may need some training steps to recover it. Since RelaxQAT has a slowly changing floating point bitwidth, this reduces sudden spikes in the loss function. Next, we explain the changes to the quantization equations needed to realize the proposed floating point bitwidth.

3.2 RelaxSEQ

QAT first replaces each model weight with its corresponding quantized-dequantized (QDQ) weight which is computed as a function of a latent floating point weight θ\theta and its channelwise scale α\alpha. Specifically, given a θ∈ℝn×m\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, the latent floating point weight with nn output channels and mm input channels and a channelwise scale α∈ℝn\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, various quantization schemes compute the QDQ weights in different ways Esser et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2025b). Then, the model is trained with the latent weight θ\theta and the scale α\alpha as the trainable parameters, where the QDQ weight is computed in every forward pass and passed on to the model layers. The associated backward pass is also modified using Straight-Through Estimators (STE), etc. Esser et al. (2019).

Recently, a popular 2-bit and sub-2-bit (e.g., ternary, 1.58-bits) scheme called Stretched Elastic Quantizer (SEQ) was proposed in ParetoQ Liu et al. (2025b). The main advantage of SEQ compared to LSQ Esser et al. (2019) for 2-bit QAT is that it results in a symmetric {−3,−1,1,3}\{-3,-1,1,3\} integer grid. In contrast, LSQ results in an aysmmetric {−2,−1,0,1}\{-2,-1,0,1\} integer grid which does not perform as well for 2-bit QAT. The QDQ weight wpw_{p} using the existing SEQ Liu et al. (2025b) is computed as:

wp=αk​{round​[clip​(θα,−1,1)×k−0.5]+0.5}.w_{p}=\frac{\alpha}{k}\left\{\text{round}\left[\text{clip}\left(\frac{\theta}{\alpha},-1,1\right)\times k-0.5\right]+0.5\right\}. (2)

Here, k=2b−1k=2^{b-1}, bb is the number of bits. In principle, we can use Eq. 1 to assign a dynamically changing, floating point bitwidth to the existing SEQ Eq. (2) because kk is a function of the number of bits. That is, the range of the QDQ weight distribution simply expands or shrinks as bb changes. Note that, wpw_{p} first performs a clipping and then rounds the resulting expression. Thus, excluding the α/k\alpha/k scaling and the +0.5+0.5 shift in Eq. (2), this Clip-then-Round operation obviously results in integer values for all the quantization bins, including the extremes. We next analyze how these extreme quantization bins vary when the bitwidth changes.

Suppose that we are given a latent weight θ∼𝒩⁡(0,0.02)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.02) and its corresponding channelwise scale α=max​{θ}\alpha=\text{max}\{\theta\}. For the purpose of this simulation, the latent weight and the scale are fixed, and only the bitwidth is reduced from 4 bits to 2 bits in Eq. (2). In Fig. 2, we plot how the extreme values of the distribution change as the schedule continues to reduce the bitwidth. Clearly, the existing SEQ (Clip-then-Round, red) shows a sudden, staircase drop in extreme integers.

Why does this sudden change in integer ranges pose a problem? During QAT, the training continues between the staircase drops assuming that those extreme integers are available. However, when btb_{t} (and thus k=2bt−1k=2^{b_{t}-1}) is reduced due to a schedule, those extreme integers suddenly disappear. In other words, during training, if the bitwidth is dynamically reduced, the model weights get finetuned assuming that we have these extreme integers. However, these extreme integers are abruptly lost as the training goes on. This loss of extreme integers can result in unstable training behavior and sudden loss spikes (similar to UPQ Lee et al. (2025)). Indeed, additional training steps are needed to recover from each loss spike. Consequently, we need to modify the existing SEQ to gradually change the extreme values in the QDQ distribution. To this end, we propose RelaxSEQ as:

wr=αk​{clip​(round​[θα×k−0.5],−k,k−1)+0.5}.w_{r}=\frac{\alpha}{k}\left\{\text{clip}\left(\text{round}\left[\frac{\theta}{\alpha}\times k-0.5\right],-k,k-1\right)+0.5\right\}. (3)

Essentially, RelaxSEQ flips the order of operations from Clip-then-Round to Round-then-Clip and makes the clipping ranges a function of kk. Therefore, when the bitwidth is floating point, the extreme values (resulting from the clipping operation) are also floating point. Meanwhile, similar to the existing SEQ, the distribution can still shrink and expand with the changing bitwidth. As a result, when the precision changes, there is a smooth change in the extreme values of the distribution, which leads to a smoothly changing loss with no sudden spikes. As ω\omega becomes 1 towards the end of the training, the model converges to the desired low-bitwidth. Fig. 2 ( green) demonstrates that as the bit schedule progresses, the extreme values smoothly change instead of a sudden staircase drop as in the existing SEQ. More details on existing SEQ vs. RelaxSEQ including some early training and benchmarking results are shown in Appendix A, Figs. 5, 6, and Table 10.

3.3 RelaxQAT

We now combine the bit schedule and the RelaxSEQ to get the proposed RelaxQAT method. We implement the bit schedule as a transformers.TrainerCallback. Algorithm 1 shows a psuedo-code to initialize the bitwidth

schedule. It requires start bits (bsb_{s}), end bits (beb_{e}), cycle start step (cs​sc_{ss}), cycle end step (ce​sc_{es}), cycle length (clc_{l}), and maximum schedule steps (msm_{s}) as arguments. Then, an array ω\omega is initialized to evenly spaced msm_{s} numbers between 0 and 1 (all inclusive). Eq. (1) is then used to obtain a list of floating point bitwidths BB. The number of full cycles nn and cycle intervals 𝒞\mathcal{C} are obtained using cs​sc_{ss}, ce​sc_{es}, and clc_{l}. Finally, for each SEQ module, various states are initialized (e.g., cycle indices, bit schedule list, bit schedule index).

After initialization, we compute the dynamic bitwidth at each training step as shown in Algorithm 2. As mentioned in Section 3.1, we start with a half cycle going from bsb_{s} to beb_{e} bits. Then we conduct nn full cycles going from beb_{e} to bsb_{s} and then back to beb_{e} bitwidth. Once all nn cycles have ended, we set the bitwidth to beb_{e} for the final finetuning in the desired bit precision. Hence, at each global step tt during training, the dynamic bitwidth btb_{t} is set using Algorithm 2. Finally, we assign the dynamic bitwidth btb_{t} to the RelaxSEQ function. The forward function shown in Algorithm 3 computes the QDQ weight wrw_{r} and sends it to the nn.Linear layers in the transformer modules. The backward function for RelaxSEQ is similar to the backward function of existing SEQ Liu et al. (2025b), except the clipping ranges are changed based on Eq. (3). This completes the description of our proposed RelaxQAT technique.

3.4 Systems Considerations

Any new QAT paradigm must not come at the expense of training speed, particularly because low-bit (2-bit or sub-2-bit) QAT requires billions of tokens in training in order to recover sufficient accuracy. To this end, we implemented triton kernels Tillet et al. (2019) for both Re-

laxSEQ and the existing ParetoQ SEQ functions. We train Qwen3-0.6B model Yang et al. (2025) on 10B tokens on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Table 1 shows the end-to-end training time for ParetoQ and RelaxQAT in GPU hours. As evident, both ParetoQ and RelaxQAT achieve very similar GPU hours with RelaxQAT being slightly faster (but within margin of error). Note that, Algorithms 1 and 2 precompute the bit schedule at initialization. Hence, the bitwdith is simply assigned to RelaxSEQ without any computation of Eq. (1) during the forward pass. This further removes any additional overhead resulting from the bit schedule in RelaxQAT.

4 Theoretical Insights

Let us now derive some simple theoretical insights for RelaxQAT. Although RelaxQAT is proposed for SEQ, the same principles apply to other quantizers such as Learned Step-size Quantizer (LSQ) Esser et al. (2019). The LSQ QDQ weight is computed as:

wl=αk​{clip​(round​[θα×k],−k,k−1)}.w_{l}=\frac{\alpha}{k}\left\{\text{clip}\left(\text{round}\left[\frac{\theta}{\alpha}\times k\right],-k,k-1\right)\right\}. (4)

Once again, k=2b−1k=2^{b-1}. It is easy to see why the same RelaxQAT ideas apply to LSQ. The main difference between Eq. (3) and (4) is the shift factor of 0.5 which changes the integer grid from {−3,−1,1,3}\{-3,-1,1,3\} for RelaxQAT to {−2,−1,0,1}\{-2,-1,0,1\} for LSQ for a 2-bit QAT. Since the LSQ grid is simpler to analyze, without loss of generality, we will use it in this section to derive our theoretical insights.

We will show two key results: (i) How is bitwidth related to the flatness of the quantization loss surface and how we may need integer changes in QDQ weights to make progress when we are stuck on a flat surface? (ii) Why does the optimization stall when the QAT does not result in a substantial change in integer values? We will also demonstrate how RelaxQAT can help with the above problems.

Proposition 1.

The higher the bit precision, the smaller the width of the quantization hyperplanes. Specifically, given two bitwidths b1b_{1} and b2b_{2}, with b1<b2b_{1}<b_{2}, the width of the quantization hyperplanes can be reduced by a factor of 2b2−b12^{b_{2}-b_{1}} if we relax the bitwidth from b1b_{1} to b2b_{2}.

Therefore, relaxing the bitwidth during QAT can help the optimization escape the flat regions in the loss surface.

Proof.

See Appendix B for the proof. ∎

We next simulate a real quantization loss surface for a toy problem to illustrate how flatness increases with larger scale values. Fig. 3(a) plots a simple 1-d function: x4−3​x3−2​xx^{4}-3x^{3}-2x. The problem is to minimize this function. Now, if we choose xx as the optimization variable, a 1-d function in the floating point domain will result in a 2-d optimization problem in the quantized realm. This is because the scalar xx splits into a scalar latent weight θ\theta and a scalar δ\delta scale. Thus, the minimization problem is wl4−3​wl3−2​wl{w_{l}}^{4}-3{w_{l}}^{3}-2{w_{l}}, where wlw_{l} comes from the LSQ Eq. (4) and {θ,δ}\{\theta,\delta\} are the two optimization variables. Fig. 3(b) shows the highly complex 2-d, 2-bit quantization loss surface arising from a simple 1-d minimization problem. As evident, we see clear quantization hyperplanes marking the integer value changes in the QDQ weight. More importantly, we see that as the scale becomes larger, the width of the hyperplanes increases, just as predicted in Proposition 1. Hence, relaxing the bitwidth (which reduces the scale δ\delta) can help a stuck optimization by reducing the width of such hyperplanes.

Fig. 3(b) also shows a red line tracing the optimization path on the quantized loss surface. It moves across multiple hyperplanes, which show changes in the integer value in the QDQ weight, to reach near the minimum point. An interesting problem then would be to understand how important these integer changes are for a QAT. Moreover, can we mathematically capture the QAT optimization trajectory (e.g., red line in Fig. 3(b))? This leads us to our next theoretical result.

Proposition 2.

The direction of the QAT trajectory is primarily decided by the scale gradients only and not by the latent weight gradients if there are no integer changes in the QDQ weight tensor. This can slow down the training convergence since there are a lot more latent weights than (channelwise) scale parameters in the model.

Since RelaxQAT relaxes the bitwidth which reduces the width of quantization hyperplanes defined by the integer-change boundaries, it makes it easier to change integers. This directly contributes to the directions the QAT trajectory can take by better utilizing the latent weight gradients, and thus results in faster convergence.

Proof.

Let us first rewrite Eq. (4) in the following form:

w(t)=δ(t)​⌊θ(t)δ(t)⌉=δ(t)​z(t),w^{(t)}=\delta^{(t)}\left\lfloor\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{\delta^{(t)}}\right\rceil=\delta^{(t)}z^{(t)}, (5)

where, w(t)w^{(t)} is the QDQ weight at training step tt, δ(t)=α(t)2b−1\delta^{(t)}=\frac{\alpha^{(t)}}{2^{b-1}} is the scale at step tt, and bb is an integer bitwidth, e.g., 2-bits. The ⌊⌉\lfloor\rceil operator should be understood as the Round-then-Clip from Eq. (4). Since bb is an integer here, z(t)z^{(t)} is the integer value of the QDQ weight at step tt.

Now, let us mathematically describe the QAT trajectory (red line in Fig. 3(b)). The QDQ weight at step t+1t+1 is given by:

w(t+1)\displaystyle w^{(t+1)} =δ(t+1)​⌊θ(t+1)δ(t+1)⌉\displaystyle=\delta^{(t+1)}\left\lfloor\frac{\theta^{(t+1)}}{\delta^{(t+1)}}\right\rceil (6)
=(δ(t)−η​dδ(t))​⌊(θ(t)−η​dθ(t))(δ(t)−η​dδ(t))⌉\displaystyle=(\delta^{(t)}-\eta d_{\delta}^{(t)})\left\lfloor\frac{(\theta^{(t)}-\eta d_{\theta}^{(t)})}{(\delta^{(t)}-\eta d_{\delta}^{(t)})}\right\rceil
=(δ(t)−η​dδ(t))​z(t+1)\displaystyle=(\delta^{(t)}-\eta d_{\delta}^{(t)})z^{(t+1)}
=δ(t)​z(t+1)−η​z(t+1)​dδ(t),\displaystyle=\delta^{(t)}z^{(t+1)}-\eta z^{(t+1)}d_{\delta}^{(t)},

where, η\eta is the learning rate, dδ(t)d_{\delta}^{(t)} (dθ(t)d_{\theta}^{(t)}) is the optimizer (e.g., Adam or SGD) update as a function of the gradient of δ\delta (θ\theta), and z(t+1)z^{(t+1)} is the integer value at step t+1t+1. Note that, the gradient information of θ\theta is contained only within z(t+1)z^{(t+1)} and does not appear anywhere else in Eq. (6). When there is no integer change at a given training step, we have:

w(t+1)\displaystyle w^{(t+1)} =δ(t)​z(t+1)−η​z(t+1)​dδ(t)\displaystyle=\delta^{(t)}z^{(t+1)}-\eta z^{(t+1)}d_{\delta}^{(t)} (7)
=δ(t)z(t)−ηz(t)dδ(t)(since z(t+1)=z(t))\displaystyle=\delta^{(t)}z^{(t)}-\eta z^{(t)}d_{\delta}^{(t)}\ \ \ \ \ (\text{since }z^{(t+1)}=z^{(t)})
=w(t)−ηz(t)dδ(t)(Eq. (5))\displaystyle=w^{(t)}-\eta z^{(t)}d_{\delta}^{(t)}\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (\text{Eq.~\eqref{eq:anotherlsq}})
=w(t)−η​dw(t),\displaystyle=w^{(t)}-\eta d_{w}^{(t)},

where, dw(t)=z(t)​dδ(t)d_{w}^{(t)}=z^{(t)}d_{\delta}^{(t)}. Hence, when the integer values zz do not change, there are no gradient directions (dθ(t)d_{\theta}^{(t)}) coming from the latent weights, and the optimization direction is primarily driven by the scales. Further, because the number of latent weights far exceed the (channelwise) scales, a lack of integer changes during QAT can slow down the training convergence. This highlights how gradual changes to the loss surface induced by RelaxQAT can lead to more integer changes, and thus meaningfully contribute to the QAT convergence by better utilizing the latent weight gradients. ∎

Finally, similar to Fig. 3(b) which was produced using LSQ, we repeat the analysis for the ParetoQ SEQ and RelaxSEQ (Eqs. (2) and (3), respectively). The loss visualization is shown in Fig. 7 in Appendix C.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

We perform experiments on Qwen3 (0.6B/4B), Qwen3.5 (2B/4B) and Gemma3-1B models in the language domain and Qwen3.5 (2B/4B) models in the vision-language domain. We compare our method against five state-of-the-art QAT baselines, including ParetoQ Liu et al. (2025b), LLM-QAT Liu et al. (2024a), UPQ Lee et al. (2025), BitNet Hugging Face (2024), and WinQ Li et al. (2026). Additionally, we evaluate AdaScale AIMET (2026), a PTQ method for comparison. For BitNet, since Hugging Face (2024) is only for 1.58 bits and has no learnable scale, we adopt ParetoQ’s SEQ function to get the 2-bit QDQ weight and use it inside the BitNet algorithm.

The training data consists of a mixture of DCLM-Edu  Allal et al. (2025), tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture  Allen Institute for AI () and xlam-function-calling-60k  Liu et al. (2024b). For vision-language model training, we additionally include Llama-Nemotron-VLM-Dataset-v1  NVIDIA (). We train all models on 10B tokens. We use the same initial learning rate of 0.0001 for all models and baselines with a cosine learning rate schedule that decays to nearly zero. The smaller models are trained on a single node of eight H100 GPUs whereas the bigger models are trained on two A100 nodes. Note that, we only do weight only quantization in all experiments.

We select n=1n=1 full cycle (after an initial half cycle) for all experiments. For maximum schedule steps msm_{s}, we perform a grid search between {400,800,1200}\{400,800,1200\}. We also conduct a detailed ablation study to show that RelaxQAT is robust across hyperparameter choices for nn and msm_{s}. Also, we set bs=4b_{s}=4 and be=2b_{e}=2 bits, signifying a 4-bit to 2-bit schedule.

In the language domain, we evaluate RelaxQAT on five zero-shot common sense reasoning tasks. These include Arc-easy, Arc-challenge  Clark et al. (2018), HellaSwag  Zellers et al. (2019), Winogrande  Sakaguchi et al. (2021), and PIQA  Bisk et al. (2020). We also report five-shot MMLU  Hendrycks et al. (2020) (loglikelihood task) and IFEval  Zhou et al. (2023) (generative task) benchmarks, each focusing on evaluating the knowledge and instruction following capabilities of the model. In vision domain, we evaluate on MMMU  Yue et al. (2024), DocVQA  Mathew et al. (2021), and ScienceQA  Lu et al. (2022) benchmarks.

5.2 Language Modeling Results

We first look at the loss convergence of RelaxQAT. Fig. 4 demonstrates the training convergence of RelaxQAT vs. ParetoQ for the Qwen3-0.6B model class. As evident, the initial half cycle from 4-bits to 2-bits significantly boosts the accuracy. However, by step 3000 or so, ParetoQ starts to catch up. The final (n=1n=1) full cycle further accelerates the RelaxQAT towards the end. Hence, RelaxQAT converges faster and achieves a significantly better training loss.

We now analyze the performance of RelaxQAT against several quantization baselines. Table 2 presents the accuracy of various quantized 2-bit Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 models on (i) five common sense reasoning datasets, (ii) their average (CSR), (iii) MMLU, (iv) IFEval, and (iv) the global average of CSR, MMLU, and IFEval. As shown, AdaScale AIMET (2026), a PTQ technique that combines leading methods like OmniQuant Shao et al. (2024) and FlexRound Lee et al. (2023), performs poorly in a 2-bit setting. In terms of QAT methods, ParetoQ achieves a global average accuracy of 69.03%. Compared to this, RelaxQAT achieves 70.03% global average accuracy (+𝟏%\bm{+1\%} over ParetoQ) and also achieves the best overall accuracy on 7/9 columns reported in Table 2 (with the second-best accuracy on the remaining two). The runner-up for the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 model class in global average is WinQ at 69.40%. We beat WinQ by 0.63%.

Next, we consider the Qwen3-0.6B to see if RelaxQAT is still effective on a smaller model. All benchmark evaluation results are shown in Table 3. Compared to ParetoQ’s 39.34% global average accuracy, we achieve a substantially higher 47.04% (+7.7%\bm{+7.7\%}) on this model class. The second-best method in Table 3 is BitNet at 45.04%. We outperform BitNet by 𝟐%\bm{2\%}. Thus, RelaxQAT outperforms even the second-best baseline by a significant margin for Qwen3-0.6B.

Let us now move on to a more recent model class: Qwen3.5-4B. Once again, Table 4 shows a significant improvement of 1.38%\bm{1.38\%} accuracy over ParetoQ. The second best is WinQ and we outperform it by 0.41%\bm{0.41\%} on average. RelaxQAT also achieves the highest or second highest scores on 8 of the 9 columns reported in Table 4. Next, we also consider the Qwen3.5-2B model and show its results in Table 5. As evident, RelaxQAT outperform ParetoQ by 0.36%\bm{0.36\%} and achieves the best or second-best scores on 6 out of 9 columns reported. The second-best method for Qwen3.5-2B is UPQ with only 0.24%0.24\% lower accuracy than RelaxQAT. UPQ achieves highest or second highest scores on 5 out of 9 columns in Table 5.

5.3 Vision-Language Modeling Results

We now present the results on vision-language problems such as MMMU, DocVQA, and ScienceQA. Table 6 shows the results for Qwen3.5-4B. Clearly, we achieve the highest or second-highest accuracy on 3 of the 4 columns. Overall, RelaxQAT achieves the second highest average accuracy which is 0.82%\bm{0.82\%} above ParetoQ, but only 0.16% below UPQ, the best performing method for this model.

For Qwen3.5-2B, the results are shown in Table 7. As evident, RelaxQAT demonstrates strong VLM performance with a massive 6.26%\bm{6.26\%} accuracy gain over ParetoQ. We also see a nearly 𝟗%\bm{9\%} gain in the ScienceQA score for RelaxQAT compared to the second-best method (UPQ). On average, RelaxQAT outperforms UPQ by a large (3.75%\bm{3.75\%}) margin.

Our results demonstrate how RelaxQAT outperforms baselines across the board for both LLM and VLM tasks. Importantly, no other single method consistently scores the highest or second-highest for all these different tasks; the second highest position is shared by WinQ, UPQ, and BitNet. This further highlights the effectiveness of RelaxQAT.

5.4 Ablations

In this section, we evaluate the impact of RelaxQAT hyperparameters such as maximum schedule steps msm_{s} and number of full cycles nn. To this end, we conduct two ablation studies using the Qwen3-0.6B model. We also show whether RelaxQAT works on model classes other than the Qwen family.

Varying 𝒎𝒔\bm{m_{s}}.

While fixing n=1n=1 full cycle after the initial half cycle of the bit schedule, we vary msm_{s} between {400,800,1200,1600,2000}\{400,800,1200,1600,2000\}. The results are shown in Table 8. We make two key observations: (a) RelaxQAT is fairly robust across different choices of maximum schedule steps. Specifically, all msm_{s} values significantly outperform ParetoQ (by 6.45%\bm{6.45\%} to 7.7%\bm{7.7\%}) and also beat the second highest BitNet method shown in Table 3. (b) The values of ms∈{400,800,1200}m_{s}\in\{400,800,1200\} typically perform the best, which is what we have used throughout this work.

Varying 𝒏\bm{n}.

Next, we change the number of full cycles n∈{0,1,2,3,4}n\in\{0,1,2,3,4\} after the initial half cycle for ms=400m_{s}=400. Table 9 shows that RelaxQAT is once again quite robust to the choice of nn since all values provide a substantial accuracy boost compared to ParetoQ (4.5%\bm{4.5\%} to 𝟕%\bm{7\%}). Moreover, n=1n=1 performs the best among all other nn values considered. Of note, RelaxQAT with n=0n=0, i.e., just the initial half cycle of bit schedule and no full cycles, outperforms ParetoQ by about 4.5%\bm{4.5\%}. Most interestingly, all non-zero full cycle cases (n≥1n\geq 1) outperform RelaxQAT with n=0n=0 by a large margin of up to nearly 2.5%\bm{2.5\%}. This demonstrates that while the initial half cycle dramatically speeds up the early convergence, further bit schedule relaxation cycles result in significant additional accuracy gains.

What about model classes outside the Qwen family?

To address this, we present results for Gemma-3-1B-it model in Table 11 in Appendix E. Once again, RelaxQAT significantly outperforms ParetoQ by 3.35%\bm{3.35\%} with highest or second highest scores in 6 out of 9 columns. Overall, RelaxQAT outperforms the second best method WinQ by 2.63%\bm{2.63\%}, a significant margin. Most notably, RelaxQAT achieves a nearly 𝟔%\bm{6\%} higher IFEval score than the second best method.

5.5 Does RelaxQAT work for Ternary Quantization?

Finally, we investigate whether RelaxQAT works for other quantization schemes such as ternary (1.58) bits: {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\} integer grid. Table 12 in Appendix F shows the accuracy of ternary Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 models. As evident, RelaxQAT performs the best with 4.2%\bm{4.2\%} higher accuracy than ParetoQ. Similar results are observed for Table 13 in Appendix F for the ternary Qwen3.5-2B model. RelaxQAT outperforms ParetoQ by 1.38%\bm{1.38\%}. Hence, RelaxQAT is a versatile technique that strongly outperforms leading methods for both ternary (1.58-bit) and 2-bit quantization.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper, we have explored a new paradigm which aims to create a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. To this end, we have proposed RelaxQAT which dynamically varies the bitwidth during training in a continuous floating point domain. RelaxQAT gradually alters the bit precision of model weights in order to accelerate the early training convergence, as well as to escape any flat regions in the low-bit quantization loss surfaces. We have also presented simple theoretical and empirical insights into why RelaxQAT helps QAT. Our extensive experiments demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 6.3%\bm{6.3\%} on vision and up to 7.7%\bm{7.7\%} on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

Finally, although we have considered weight only quantization in this work, RelaxQAT can also be applied to activation or KV-cache quantization. We leave this for future work.

7 AI Usage Disclosure

No AI was used in ideation, literature search, experiment design, code implementation, and writing of this paper. Supplementary Information: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training

Appendix A Existing SEQ vs. RelaxSEQ

Let us now look at some concrete loss and test accuracy behavior for the existing ParetoQ SEQ Liu et al. (2025b) (Clip-then-Round) vs. the proposed RelaxSEQ (Round-then-Clip) when trained under a specific bitwidth schedule. As mentioned before, existing SEQ (due to Clip-then-Round) loses extreme integers as the schedule reduces bitwidth from bsb_{s} to beb_{e} bits. In contrast, RelaxSEQ results in a smoothly changing extreme values. Our hypothesis is that the sudden change in extreme integers can cause the loss to spike.

We noticed this issue early on during the development of RelaxQAT. Specifically, we show the unstable behavior of existing SEQ (Clip-then-Round) in Fig. 5 for an early train-

ing run for the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 model. In contrast, RelaxSEQ has a smoothly changing loss. Interestingly, we noticed that although Clip-then-Round shows loss spikes and unstable training, the final loss did recover and perform similarly to RelaxSEQ. However, we found that Clip-then-Round resulted in poor benchmark scores as shown in Table 10. Consequently, we chose RelaxSEQ (Eq. (3)) as our main QDQ equation in this work.

Figs. 6(a-d) continue the analysis from Section 3.2. Using the same simulation environment from Fig. 2, we show how the weight distribution changes with bitwidth for the existing SEQ equation. As k=2b−1k=2^{b-1} shrinks with decreasing bitwidth, the weight distribution also narrows. However, the extreme values do not change until the argument to the round operation becomes sufficiently small. When kk becomes sufficiently small, the extreme integers are suddenly lost. For instance, in Figs. 6(a-d), the extreme integer values go from {−15,15}\{-15,15\} to {−13,−13}\{-13,-13\} and so on (see dotted red lines). This happens because in the existing SEQ equation, even if the bitwidth can be varied and is floating point, the extremes are still integers due to the Clip-then-Round operation.

Figs. 6(e-h) illustrate the intermediate floating point extreme values for RelaxSEQ. The extreme values for floating point bitwidths are floating points, yet all other intermediate quantization bins are integers.

Appendix B Proof of Proposition 1

Proposition 1.

The higher the bit precision, the smaller the width of the quantization hyperplanes. Specifically, given two bitwidths b1b_{1} and b2b_{2}, with b1<b2b_{1}<b_{2}, the width of the quantization hyperplanes can be reduced by a factor of 2b2−b12^{b_{2}-b_{1}} if we relax the bitwidth from b1b_{1} to b2b_{2}.

Therefore, relaxing the bitwidth during QAT can help the optimization escape the flat regions in the loss surface.

Proof.

Consider the LSQ Eq. (4) and let δ=αk=α2b−1\delta=\frac{\alpha}{k}=\frac{\alpha}{2^{b-1}}. Then, the argument to the round operation becomes θδ\frac{\theta}{\delta}. Note that, the round operation decides the boundaries of the quantization bins. Given a current integer value ziz_{i}, let us assume that the adjacent quantization bins lead to integers zi−1z_{i-1} and zi+1z_{i+1}. Suppose that θδ\frac{\theta}{\delta} is at the center of the quantization bin for the integer ziz_{i}. Then, the minimum movement in θδ\frac{\theta}{\delta} to reach the neighboring quantization bins zi−1z_{i-1} or zi+1z_{i+1} would be 0.50.5. For example, if zi−1=−1z_{i-1}=-1, zi=0z_{i}=0, and zi+1=+1z_{i+1}=+1, and θδ=0\frac{\theta}{\delta}=0, we need to move it by 0.50.5 to reach the neighboring quantization boundaries. This is because θδ∈(−0.5,0.5)\frac{\theta}{\delta}\in(-0.5,0.5) still results in zi=0z_{i}=0, θδ=−0.5\frac{\theta}{\delta}=-0.5 leads to zi−1=−1z_{i-1}=-1, and θδ=0.5\frac{\theta}{\delta}=0.5 leads to zi+1=+1z_{i+1}=+1.

Therefore, the latent weight θ\theta must move by 0.5​δ0.5\delta from the center of the quantization bin to change the integer value in the resulting QDQ weight. Hence, the width of the quantization hyperplane (defined by the flat region where the integer value does not change) is given by =2×0.5​δ=δ=2\times 0.5\delta=\delta.

Now, since δ=α2b−1\delta=\frac{\alpha}{2^{b-1}}, the higher the bit precision, the smaller the delta, which in turn results in a smaller width of the quantization hyperplanes. Specifically, if we relax the bitwidth from b1b_{1} to b2b_{2} bits (b1<b2b_{1}<b_{2}), we get:

δ1δ2=α2b1−1α2b2−1=2b2−b1⟹δ2=δ12b2−b1\frac{\delta_{1}}{\delta_{2}}=\frac{\frac{\alpha}{2^{b_{1}-1}}}{\frac{\alpha}{2^{b_{2}-1}}}=2^{b_{2}-b_{1}}\implies\delta_{2}=\frac{\delta_{1}}{2^{b_{2}-b_{1}}} (8)

That is, the width of the quantization hyperplanes reduces by a factor of 2b2−b12^{b_{2}-b_{1}}. As a result, if the QAT optimization is stuck in a flat region, dynamically and gradually relaxing the bitwidth can reduce the width of the quantization hyperplanes and enable the QAT to escape those flat regions. ∎

Appendix C SEQ Simulation

We start again with a 1-d optimization problem which becomes 2-d for the quantized domain. For RelaxQAT, we also implement a bit schedule to see how a changing loss surface alters the optimization trajectory. For ParetoQ, the number of bits are fixed to 2-bits. Figs. 7(a-d) show that ParetoQ gets stuck near the true minimum and does not reach it even with many more (10000) training steps. In contrast, Fig. 7(e-h) converges within the 2000 steps because the initial changing loss surface sets the optimization on a different path.

We notice similar convergence patterns on real LLM/VLM trainings (see Fig. 4 in the main paper) where (i) the initial convergence accelerates significantly due to changing integers during the first half cycle of the bit schedule, and (ii) Further nn cycles help the optimization escape the flatter regions in the loss surface.

Appendix D More Details on Experiments

We use a total batch size of 256 for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B and Gemma3-1B and a batch size of 320 for Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B models. We implement the AdamW optimizer with zero weight decay.

For evaluation, we select a variety of tasks. For instance, common sense reasoning (CSR) benchmarks include five tasks: Arc-easy, Arc-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA and WinoGrande which focus on everyday knowledge tasks, grade-school science questions and plausibility. We also evaluate on benchmarks such as MMLU and IFEval. MMLU evaluates the model on factual recall and basic reasoning across 57 subjects whereas IFEval evaluates whether the model is following natural language instructions. While the CSR and MMLU tasks are multiple-choice questions, comparing the log-likelihood of each answer, IFEval is a generation task. We report accuracy norm metric for Arc-Easy, Arc-Challenge, Hellaswag, PIQA and accuracy for WingoGrande. IFEval reports four metrics namely prompt-level-strict-acc, inst-level-strict-acc, prompt-level-loose-acc, inst-level-loose-acc. For our experiments, we take an average of all four metrics.

Appendix F Ternary Quantization Results

The ternary (1.58-bit) RelaxSEQ equation is given as:

wr=αk​{clip​(round​[θα×k],−k+0.5,k−0.5)}.w_{r}=\frac{\alpha}{k}\left\{\text{clip}\left(\text{round}\left[\frac{\theta}{\alpha}\times k\right],-k+0.5,k-0.5\right)\right\}. (9)

Here, at the end of the schedule, k=2be−1=21.58−1≈1.5k=2^{b_{e}-1}=2^{1.58-1}\approx 1.5. Hence, the QDQ weight wrw_{r} achieves the ternary {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\} integer grid. Of note, during training, we vary the bit schedule from bs=3b_{s}=3 bits to be=1.58b_{e}=1.58 bits.
